processing: A green tea made from the local Damianbai cultivar. The details of firing and shaping are little documented; as with other Chinese greens, the leaf is fixed with heat, rolled and dried.
harvest_season: Exact dates are little documented. Grade follows tenderness of the fresh leaf: Yinhao is the most tender, then Maojian, then Cuifeng. As with other Jiangxi greens, this points to spring picking.
appearance_dry: Sturdy, even, straight strands so thickly covered in white down that the top grade looks snow white.
appearance_liquor: Bright and clear. The exact shade is little documented; typically a pale green-yellow for its class.
taste_profile: A high, clear aroma and a fresh, full flavour.

brewing.notes: Use a glass so you can watch the buds move. Heavy down clouds the liquor a little, which is normal for downy greens.

vintage_note: Usually sold, like other Chinese greens, as the current spring's harvest, best drunk within about a year. Look for the grade on the pack: Yinhao, Maojian or Cuifeng, in descending tenderness. It is not a tea for ageing.
description:
Shangrao Baimei is a traditional speciality green from Shangrao in northeast Jiangxi, and its name, white eyebrow, says what makes it distinct. The strands are so downy that they are compared to the white brows of an old man.

It is made from Shangrao Damianbai, a local cultivar, and the strands come out sturdy and even with a glossy green under the white. Three grades follow leaf tenderness: Yinhao, Maojian and Cuifeng.

The cup is described as high and clear in aroma, fresh and full in flavour, with tender green leaf at the bottom. Yinhao is the showpiece, snow white when dry and lively in the glass. Slightly cooled water suits it, as it does most downy greens.

Buy by grade and harvest year. Little is published on how much the grades differ in the cup, so a small sample of Yinhao beside Maojian is the honest way to find out if the price gap is worth it.
history: Shangrao Baimei is described as a traditional local tea, though little is documented about when it began. Its recorded honours are more recent: a Ministry of Agriculture quality award in 1985 and a gold medal at the second China Agricultural Expo in 1995, when it was also named a Chinese famous tea. It also appears among Jiangxi's agricultural geographical indication products.
